opus-5.5.text:
That's a good question, because I don't think I realized it at the time. Looking back, a lot of what I did as a kid was tinkering without anyone telling me what the "right" approach was. Taking things apart, trying to build little gadgets, writing small programs before I really understood what programming was. There was no curriculum for it. You just had a problem, something you wanted to work, and you'd poke at it until it did, or until you understood why it didn't.

What that taught me, I think, is that not having a framework isn't the same as being stuck. When there's no established method, you're forced to build your own mental model from scratch. You make a guess, you test it, it fails, and the failure tells you something. That loop of hypothesize, try, observe, adjust became really natural to me before I had the vocabulary for it.

It also taught me comfort with being confused for a while. A lot of people, when they hit a problem that doesn't fit a textbook pattern, feel anxious. But if you've spent your childhood in that state, confusion just feels like the beginning of the interesting part.

Later, in research, and especially in robotics, that turned out to matter a lot. The real world doesn't come with a framework. A robot fails in some way nobody anticipated, and there's no chapter that tells you why. So I'd say those early years gave me a kind of confidence. Not that I'd always find the answer, but that I could find *a* way in, even when nobody had drawn the map yet.

r001.rationale: The response describes developing confidence to find a way into problems with no established method or map, recognizing this as a personal strength.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a good question, because I think a lot of what I do now in robotics research is really about that: what happens when you hand a system a problem and there's no recipe for it.

Growing up, I didn't have much structure around learning outside of school. School itself was very framework-heavy, especially in the Chinese system. There's a right way to solve each kind of problem, you drill it, you get fast at recognizing which template applies. And I was decent at that. But honestly, the things that stuck with me came from outside the classroom, where nobody was telling me what the template was.

I remember tinkering with computers as a kid, mostly because things broke and there wasn't anyone around who could fix them. So you poke at it. You change one thing, see what happens, change it back, try something else. It's embarrassingly unprincipled, but you build this intuition that a problem is not a wall, it's a collection of smaller things you can test. And you learn to be okay sitting in a state where you genuinely don't know what's going on for a while. I think that tolerance for confusion is maybe the most important thing I picked up before eighteen.

The other piece is that when you don't have a framework, you have to invent a proxy for progress. There's no answer key. So you start asking, what would convince me I'm closer? Can I get a smaller version of this working? That habit maps almost directly onto research. When you're building a robot that has to manipulate objects in a messy kitchen, there's no textbook chapter for that. You have to decompose it yourself, decide what the first experiment is, and accept that your decomposition might be wrong.

So if I'm honest, I'd say those early experiences taught me less that I'm good at solving problems without a framework, and more that the framework is something you construct on the way. You don't wait for one. You build a crappy one, use it until it breaks, and then build a better one. That's basically what I still do, just with more compute.

r001.rationale: The candidate identifies tolerance for confusion and the ability to build and revise a framework while working through an uncertain problem as personal strengths developed early in life.

astra-6.text:
I think they taught me that I don’t need to have the whole framework figured out before I start. When you’re young, you often don’t know what the standard approach is, so you try something, see what happens, and adjust. There’s a kind of freedom in that.

But I wouldn’t say the lesson was that I can solve everything on my own. It was more that I can make progress even when I don’t know exactly what I’m doing yet. I can ask questions, learn what I’m missing, and gradually give the problem some structure. That makes uncertainty feel less like a reason to stop.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a personal ability to make progress when there is no established approach, learn what is missing, and gradually structure the problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they taught me that I don’t need to know the whole path before I start. When you’re young, you often haven’t learned the established way of doing something, so you try things, make mistakes, and adjust. There’s a kind of freedom in that.

But I wouldn’t say it means solving problems without any structure. It’s more about being able to create structure when nobody gives it to you: What do I know? What am I missing? What’s one thing I can try? That gives me confidence that even if I don’t know how to solve a problem yet, I can start figuring it out.

r001.rationale: The response describes confidence in starting with uncertainty and creating structure when no established way is provided, conveying a personal strength in solving problems without a framework.
